This study aims to identify the first known case of a single RL AGN successfully driving the feedback process responsible for retaining a significant hot gas component within an ETG. We examined NGC 4698, a Coma Cluster ETG featuring a well-characterized hot gas halo, detailed X-ray observations indicating active feedback driving buoyant shocks through its intracluster medium, and strong radio emission (5 jy at 1.4 GHz) linked to a point-like non-nuclear radio galaxy. Spectroscopic data confirm that this AGN is RL and exhibits Coma Cluster clustericity. Our analysis demonstrates that the hot gas' specific entropy increases radially in shocks with an average speed of approximately 11 km/s, yielding X-ray luminosity and entropy profiles that align closely with theoretical models of star-forming late-type GALs. By linking the AGN's power output to the dynamics of the outer X-ray emitting gas, we find that the ratio of feedback energy injection to the AGN's radiative energy lies between 10^3 and 10^4. Consequently, we conclude that NGC 4698 represents the inaugural example of hot gas feedback mechanisms within an ETG that appears to be sustained by a RL AGN. The existence of such systems implies a minimal efficiency of $\sim$0.01% for RL AGN feedback within ETGs. While this figure is lower than efficiencies estimated for star-forming galaxies, the discovery of NGC 4698 proves that all these feedback modes can coexist across different galaxy types.

The primary objective is to reconstruct a compactly supported source term from a finite set of measurements of the associated solution. This reconstruction capability relies on demonstrating the localized dependence of the global IP operator by establishing an a priori bound on the local Lipschitz norm of the local inverse operator. This process involves compressing feature vectors from a global descriptor, filtered by semantic cues, into a single representation. Historically, average pooling has been the dominant method, though recent trends increasingly favor max pooling and hybrid approaches. This study examines how target class frequency and data augmentation influence the performance of average-pooled semantic feature vectors. Our results indicate that frequent targets are over-represented in batch-generated feature vectors compared to rare and unseen ones. We propose that this bias stems from average pooling acting as a low-pass filter during the final layer's linear computation, which suppresses high-frequency variations more rapidly. Consequently, average pooling generates feature vectors that are biased toward frequent targets and less capable of distinguishing rare and novel ones. To validate this, we compare various global pooling techniques and demonstrate that high-pass averaged pooling and max pooling are more effective at capturing features of rare and novel objects. Furthermore, we introduce a novel high-pass pooling method derived through frequency-domain analysis, which surpasses both standard average and max pooling, as well as recent state-of-the-art alternatives. Finally, we apply these findings to neural network compression via quantization-aware training, showing that high-pass averaged pooling enables more aggressive quantization without significant accuracy loss. This allows for larger networks to be trained within fixed quantization budgets, achieving superior performance compared to fully-precision networks of similar size. Experimental validations using ImageNet classification and NCU recognition datasets confirm that high-pass pooling techniques enhance classification performance. Specifically, high-pass averaged pooling surpasses the 24-bit average-pooled state-of-the-art networks: ResNet-101 and ResNet-50+FP16Det, within the same parameter budget. Notably, this advantage is more pronounced regarding rare and novel objects. We demonstrate that even simpler high-pass pooling strategies yield significantly better performance than 24-bit average-pooled networks of equal size. Our code is available at https://github.com/fengyao12/HighPassPooling.

These approaches overcome the limitations of reliance, which suffers from measurement inaccuracy and the impossibility of detecting privately deleted links. We introduce a model that successfully rotation curve shapes by integrating two key mechanisms: self-regulated gas accretion driven by cooling and angular momentum conservation during infall. This approach allows us to predict the baryon content of isolated and star-forming galaxies. Using this model, we constructed synthetic galaxies for the MaNGA M* GALaxy NGC Survey (M*GALS) to investigate how accurately the relationship between the mass-to-luminosity ratio and inner rotation curve slope can serve as a bulk estimator for dark matter. Our findings indicate that bulk estimators rely heavily on specific assumptions, particularly that the majority of a galaxy's gas is confined to the central region. While bulk gas mass fractions exhibit a clear dependence on the inner rotation curve slope, bulk dark matter fractions do not, as the spatial distribution of dark matter is minimally affected by angular momentum during infall. Consequently, bulk estimators of the mass-to-luminosity ratio and inner dark matter fraction exhibit significant biases when applied to observed galaxies. In contrast, local estimators assume a more complex structure, requiring separate measurements of local gas mass and density profiles. Local estimators of the mass-to-luminosity ratio correlate with the inner rotation curve slope, whereas local dark matter fraction estimators do not. When applying both local and bulk estimators to M*GALS galaxies, we find local gas mass fractions to be approximately three times higher than those derived from H2 spectroscopy, a discrepancy we attribute to the capture of angular momentum by the dark halo. This suggests that the difference between local and bulk estimators of the mass-to-luminosity ratio is primarily driven by the misestimation of local gas mass fractions. Our proposed self-regiated in-fall model offers a framework to interpret various aspects of the surface and volume structure of isolated and star-forming galaxies. However, validating this model and its implications for the physical nature of the dark halo demands more precise and extensive data, including detailed baryon surface and volume distributions. Future investigations should incorporate these details to assess the reliability of current estimates of the mass-to-luminosity ratio and inner dark matter fraction. Policy gradients (PG) serve as a foundational RL approach for learning policies via environmental interactions, while Q-learning represents a parallel method designed to acquire value functions. Although both methods and various hybrid variations have been extensively studied, an essential question remains: which approach offers superior performance and scalability? To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study examining a broad spectrum of configurations across diverse tasks and settings. Our results indicate that Q-learning scales more effectively and outperforms PG in certain scenarios. Specifically, in large off-policy learning situations where prior experience data exists, Q-learning achieves faster convergence and higher sample efficiency. Conversely, PG demonstrates superior scalability in large sample-size on-policy settings. Notably, Q-learning proves scalable even in massive off-policy scenarios, such as those encountered in large-scale recommendation systems. These findings suggest that Q-learning is well-suited for large off-policy tasks, including those in recommendation systems, and we provide an open-source implementation tailored to this domain. Overall, these conclusions support established theoretical insights regarding the scalability of reinforcement learning algorithms.

The growing diversity and complexity of embedded software necessitates advanced testing methods, such as fault injection, which enables the assessment of software robustness by introducing random or targeted defects. However, traditional testing techniques often struggle to execute fault injection due to issues like control-flow disruption, random memory access, and insufficient stack depth. This paper introduces RCEFSM, a novel fault injection framework designed for resource-constrained embedded systems. Built upon a real-time cloud-enabled fault summary machine (rCSFM), RCEFSM allows for the remote administration of embedded devices, facilitating large-scale fault injection experiments that include automated analysis. By integrating fault summary machines with cloud computing, RCEFSM supports both horizontal scaling for increased processing power and vertical scaling for specific services. The system has been deployed on a private educational network connecting seven laboratories; while these nodes will serve as additional physical fault injection models, they will also provide administrative interfaces for managing and monitoring the framework. Furthermore, the paper presents initial evaluations indicating that RCEFSM can enhance fault coverage for fault-aware testing in small systems. Although RCEFSM was designed to address the specific limitations of embedded environments, it offers a fresh perspective on fault injection methodology with significant potential applications in fields beyond traditional embedded system development. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to more realistic software validation and improve the understanding of system reliability within the embedded industry.

This work investigates product spaces arising from Cayley graphs of finite groups, specifically $G_1\times G_2$, and products involving three or more such spaces. We demonstrate that for any Cayley graph of a direct product of two groups, a significant portion of vertices—at least a quarter—can be embedded into $l_2$ with an optimal worst-case distortion matching the known lower bound derived from the product theorem of Assouad, Naor, and Teliban. This paper presents a novel algorithm named compressive principal component analysis (CPCA), designed to estimate the top few principal components and their associated variances from high-dimensional data. Built upon the methodology of principal component regression (PCR), CPCA is a straightforward, efficient, and effective technique capable of accurately estimating key features of high-dimensional datasets. As a batch learning approach, CPCA demonstrates robust performance across various scenarios and can be easily extended to online learning environments. The study details the theoretical foundations of CPCA, offering precise conditions for its successful deployment; specifically, the method remains effective even when the number of samples is significantly lower than the dimensionality. Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate these theoretical predictions and illustrate the performance of CPCA. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of CPCA's performance relative to existing methods.

Specifically, we investigate the scenario where noise affects opinion-distribution asymmetry by assigning a higher noise magnitude to the minority holding the less popular opinion. We analyze this asymmetric noisy voter model analytically across various noise configurations and subsequently explore its implications for sustaining opinion pluralism through a symmetry-breaking mechanism. Although this specific scenario may not be a frequent occurrence in nature, it could serve as a component in more complex systems that ascribe noise to less popular opinions.

We demonstrate that for any such sentence $\Phi$, there exists a corresponding sentence $\Phi'$ utilizing the same variable count but relying solely on one symmetric binary relation, such that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is either identical to or strictly larger than that of $\Phi$. Furthermore, in scenarios where the original sentence requires three variables, this "reduction" can be executed without altering the number of variables required; otherwise, an increase is necessary. Finally, we provide an algorithm to construct $\Phi'$ given $\Phi$, and we analyze the computational complexity associated with this process. Notably, if $\Phi$ is expressed with minimal redundancy, then $\Phi'$ will also exhibit minimal redundancy. Additionally, we establish that the spectrum of $\Phi$ is strictly greater than that of $\Phi'$ and present an algorithm to generate a model that confirms this distinction. To illustrate the capabilities of $\Phi'$, we apply it to resolve the isomorphism problem for structures within a specific complexity class known as REC$_k$, which encompasses all sentences in $\text{D}_k$ whose finite models possess at least three elements (where $k \geq 1$). Specifically, for any structure $\mathfrak{A}$ and any sentence $\Phi$ in REC$_k$, we demonstrate that $\mathfrak{A} \models \Phi$ if and only if $\text{Aut}(\mathfrak{A})^+ \models \Phi'$, where $\text{Aut}(\mathfrak{A})^+$ denotes the group of even permutations of the automorphism group of $\mathfrak{A}$. This application highlights the significance of "half automorphisms" for REC$_k$, a concept previously utilized in related research. To support this application, we also employ a "mini-max" theorem and establish a "max-mini" theorem as its dual. Moreover, we explore an analogous application for the complexity class IND$_k$, which consists of sentences in $\text{D}_k$ featuring at least one interpretation of a reflexive relation. In this context, we show that a sentence $\Phi$ belonging to either IND$_{k+1}$ or REC$_{k+1}$ can be translated into a equivalent sentence $\Phi^*$ using the same number of variables, such that $\Phi^*$ relies exclusively on a single symmetric binary relation. While a straightforward arrangement of the unit sphere can be solved using standard linear algebra, our proposed method leverages the unit sphere's freedom of rotation to enhance computational efficiency. Specifically, we demonstrate that the time complexity of solving a sphere arrangement problem is $O(m \cdot n^{(m+1)/2})$, where $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. This represents an improvement over conventional linear algebra approaches, which typically require $O(n^3)$ operations. Furthermore, we extend this algorithm to determine all potential positions of the unit sphere given $n$ spheres, maintaining the same computational complexity. This capability has broad applications in the decomposition of space by spheres and is also pertinent to the development of sphere-deformation methods within the sphere deformation theory of space. Finally, we outline the extension process and discuss its implications for unit sphere arrangement problems. By analyzing the signs of specific constants within the derived formula, we can identify which spheres are externally and internally tangent to the unit sphere, thereby solving the problem of counting the positions of a unit sphere externally tangent to $n$ given spheres. This work complements the decomposition of space by spheres and holds significance in unit sphere arrangement problems. Our findings indicate that the computational complexity for this task is $O(m(n^2+m)^2)$. In a subsequent paper, we will demonstrate how to simplify the formula to achieve an efficiency of $O(n^2+m)$. This research builds upon our decomposition theory, the expansion of sphere radii to infinity, and the derivation of algebraic conditions for sphere non-overlapping, all of which are essential for advancing the decomposition theory of space by spheres, particularly in the context of the coloring problem. Building on projection theory, which decomposes functions into orthogonal components to approximate or extend them, we develop a novel approach for extending predictive distributions to incorporate unmeasured or latent variables. We enhance predictive models by integrating information from latent variables derived from a working predictive model through the orthogonal component, utilizing standard optimization to combine these elements. We introduce regularized versions of this method to manage overfitted models or incompatible components by ensuring orthogonality relative to a smoother space. Both theoretical and simulation studies demonstrate that regularizing latent variable extensions with predictive models regularized via the same theory yields more accurate inferences. Furthermore, we extend this regularized framework to handle multivariate responses; unlike existing methods that produce empty or degenerate projections in multivariate settings, our approach guarantees non-empty, non-degenerate projections. Across various response types, extending predictive models with latent variables multivariately results in superior inference compared to using the original model. Additionally, we apply this method to extend frequentist predictive estimates within an A/B testing framework. This process constructs regularized Frequentist Augmented Minimax (RFAM) estimates that combine data-driven predictive estimates with latent information, producing less biased outcomes under model misspecification. Extensive simulations indicate that RFAM reduces bias without increasing variance. Finally, we employ regularized techniques to improve upon default fitted and integrated Gaussian process models in functional regression for time series data. Extending this to latent variables reduces mean squared prediction errors for both responses and forecasts. We also provide an analogous functional extension to regularize unmeasured components for multivariate functional responses. Extending these models reveals structural insights, enabling the construction of better predictive models from latent information even when component models are incorrect. In multiple regression and multivariately structured time series data, the methods successfully identify interactions. During functional binary regression with 2D data, they uncover circle-shaped interactions. For bivariate and time series extensions, the method reduces mean squared errors for predictions and responses. In bivariate extensions with microsatellite data, the method identifies more structure and includes previously unexplained variation. For A/B testing, RFAM generates more precise estimates across diverse scenarios. In all cases, latent variable extensions perform equivalently to or better than regularized component models. to adversarial examples (AEs), which are intentionally modified inputs designed to deceive machine learning models. While numerous prior approaches have sought to generate such adversarial inputs, these methods typically rely on optimization techniques that are computationally and temporally costly. Consequently, they hinder the broader adoption of AE generation, particularly within high-throughput environments. To address this limitation, we introduce the self-adversarial (SA) network model. SAs utilize a generator network to create data manifolds and an discriminator network to identify them. Specifically, SA networks produce adversarial examples that successfully "fool" the discriminator at test time. We implemented both convolutional (CSA) and fully connected (FFSA) variants of this model. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed CSA and FFSA architectures can automatically learn to generate adversarial examples for target networks without requiring any manual tuning. Furthermore, our models achieve superior performance in terms of both accuracy and adversarial example generation rates compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Lastly, we validated the utility of SAs by applying them to data augmentation tasks. Tests across various datasets, including ImageNet and object detection benchmarks like PASCAL VOC and COCO, indicate that using SA-augmented data in target models enhances robustness against attacks while maintaining high accuracy. Source code for our models is available at https://github.com/zhengyif/SA-Networks.

Claims are central units within the discourse of climate change denial. Their rapid propagation across digital platforms poses a substantial challenge to effective communication strategies. While maintaining awareness of the scale and nature of this problematic content is vital for policymakers, communicators, and researchers, developing automated tools to detect and measure such claims remains difficult. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a deep content analysis tool capable of distinguishing between claims that align with scientific consensus and those that do not. We constructed and trained a neural network model using over 10,000 claims sourced from platforms including Twitter, YouTube, and Facebook. We contend that the model achieves a high degree of accuracy, operating within full precision and recall metrics of 0.91. Our results indicate that deep content analysis can effectively identify and differentiate between claims concerning the causes, consequences, and solutions of climate change. These findings have significant implications for communicating the consensus on global warming and suggest that this analytical method can be adapted to examine controversial issues in other fields. All code and datasets required to reproduce these findings are available through an open-access GitHub repository.

This study investigates the accelerated particles responsible for a notable type-I storm recorded on October 1, 2003, utilizing data from the Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imager (RHESSI) and SOHO/MDI. RHESSI detected a strong high-energy X-ray beam extending from the sunspot penumbra over a scale of approximately 10 arcseconds, resulting from the beam-beam plasma model. By analyzing RHESSI data across nine time intervals, we determined that the X-ray beam's intensity and hardness varied without a clear trend. We hypothesize that high-magnetic-energy particles generated by magnetic energy reconfiguration in the penumbra drove the observed X-ray beam characteristics. Utilizing R/HD code, we calculated the radiation from these high-magnetic-energy particles and found that the beam-beam instability theory can explain the intensity of the type-I noise storm associated with the high-energy X-ray beam. Additionally, MDI/HMI data revealed that the penumbral Brz magnetic field was weaker than field values predicted by our RHD simulations, suggesting that the noise storm was not directly caused by penumbral magnetic field reconfiguration. Therefore, we propose that the magnetic field for penumbra beam-beam instability is a penumbra field formed by the mixing of penumbral and photospheric fields. Our results indicate that penumbra beam-beam instability is more likely to accelerate particles over scales ranging from tens of arcseconds to several degrees. We further suggest that the double-strapped S-shaped structure commonly observed in type-I noise storms forms due to the interaction between the penumbra Brz magnetic field and the helicity of the solar rotation field. Finally, we conclude that the initial position of the left-hand string in this structure is not fixed at the beam footpoint in the penumbra but can exist anywhere between tens of arcseconds to several degrees away from it. This finding offers a new perspective on the formation mechanism of type-I solar noise storms. This research also has implications for the acceleration of charged particles driving solar energetic particle events and coronal mass ejections in both solar and astrophysical contexts. In the perturbative regime, we demonstrate that surface gravitational corrections arise at first order and are proportional to the shell's mass, occurring at the same order as geometric deformation parameters. Both perturbative and non-perturb surface gravitational states exhibit a dependence on both deformation and undistorted shell parameters. Furthermore, we show that the surface state can be induced by the collapse of an entire massive shell rather than just a first-order perturbation, revealing a dual role for the shell: acting as both a source and a probe of gravitational states. Finally, we establish that the total mass and angular momentum of the asymptotically flat spacetime are conserved during the formation of the surface state from the SZCH shell. Consistent with prior findings, we observe that the bulk remains asymptotically flat post-collision, while the surface becomes slightly curved; however, these respective curvatures are interrelated. These results support the black hole complementarity view that gravitational degrees of freedom are partitioned between the bulk and the horizon during black hole formation from a spherically symmetric shell. Additionally, we find that the derived surface state includes Reebound-type modes, offering a potential explanation for information recovery during black hole evaporation. These insights may aid in elucidating the fundamental building blocks of holographic dualities. These conclusions reinforce the view that the complete set of surface and bulk gravitational degrees of freedom, constructed from the SZCH shell, are essential for building a consistent black hole scenario that resolves the information paradox. Consequently, the SZCH shell serves as a viable non-singular gravitational source for the holographic description of a black hole. This work also provides new insights into the membrane paradigm and the membrane's degrees of freedom. These findings indicate that surface gravitational degrees of freedom can be accessed through bulk gravity via the Kazarnowski-Kalosh-Smirnov-Wilson (KKSM) duality. The implications of these results for the firework model and its relevance to gravitational wave observations are discussed in related literature. This paper introduces a new channel estimator designed for IEEE 802.11p-based NLOS vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications, grounded in the analysis of actual experimental channel impulse responses (CIRs). Our proposed method outperforms both the standard IEEE 802.11p channel estimator and a minimum-norm estimator, which is widely used in other non-coherent experimental estimators. The estimator leverages a specific characteristic of NLOS CIRs: the presence of narrow-band non-dispersive channels, such as underground valleys or dense urban settings. These channels typically manifest as single narrow peaks within the captured 802.11p CIRs. By modeling these peaks using a super-Gaussian distribution, the estimator achieves a significant reduction in noise influence, thereby enhancing channel coherence. Furthermore, an optimal parameter for the super-Gaussian distribution is identified and evaluated. Using a dataset of 159 actual NLOS CIRs from the IEEE 802.11p V2V channel database, we observe that our approach reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of channel coherence by 40% compared to the existing IEEE estimator and by 18% compared to the minimum-norm estimator. Additionally, we introduce a novel channel coherence metric tailored for NLOS conditions. Results indicate that this surrogate coherence aligns more accurately with reliable channel coherence than the traditional IEEE definition. Finally, simulations demonstrate that incorporating this surrogate coherence as a feedback parameter from the receiver to the transmitter can boost physical layer throughput by up to 25% in NLOS V2V scenarios. A supplementary online file provides detailed explanations and calculations using the actual NLOS CIRs extracted from measurement databases. Although music information retrieval (MIR) is an established field, the rise of procedural generative systems (PFGS) capable of creating original music in various styles sparked renewed interest. However, a significant hurdle remains in producing coherent compositions when combining multiple genres. This work revisits the problem of music genre tagging to offer solutions for procedural generation applications. We propose training a BERT language model on music scores annotated with genre labels. During generation, the model functions as a classifier for incomplete scores, enabling the blending of several music genres in PFGS outputs by adjusting tagging probabilities. We evaluate our approach using original datasets comprising classical, gospel, popular, and film music scores, alongside standard MIR benchmarks. Results demonstrate that our method achieves high accuracy in genre tagging and successfully generates plausible musical snippets at the bar level that blend multiple genres. Furthermore, single-genre procedural generative systems produced output of comparable quality to human compositions in many categories. Finally, we provide an interactive audio example on our project's website. To support reproducibility, we release the datasets and code under a CC BY 4.0 license. While our implementation includes limitations, these can be addressed through future enhancements to the underlying BERT model or the integration of additional features into the PFGS. Ultimately, this research highlights remaining challenges in music generation and paves the way for accessing genre blending techniques for the procedural music community. Additionally, the methodologies and insights gained from addressing the genre tagging task may serve as a reference for similar classification tasks in other procedural generative domains. Procedural generative systems for music often struggle to produce coherent compositions when blending multiple genres. This paper introduces a method to overcome this limitation by leveraging a language model trained on musical notation to handle genre classification. By utilizing genre labels, the proposed method enables the creation of musical excerpts that blend several genres. We employ BERT, a state-of-the-art transformer-based language model, which demonstrates significant language modeling capabilities even on extremely sparse musical data. Experimental results confirm the approach's effectiveness in genre classification and show that the resulting classification probabilities can be directly applied to generate multi-genre excerpts. Our findings indicate that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to established methods in MIR for genre classification. Furthermore, audio evaluations reveal that our generated excerpts are of high quality and that the procedural generative output is perceptually similar to human compositions in many cases. Unlike traditional ANN training approaches that rely on backpropagation, our approach utilizes an approximate random perturbation method combined with least-squares minimization. This framework is part of a broader methodology for estimating probability distribution parameters from finite, noisy data under random measurement errors. Because solving the linear system required to update parameters is native to Gaussian nuclei measurement errors and does not necessitate multiple matrix passes, measurements and simulations can be executed in parallel. We evaluated this numerical method by comparing it with backpropagation, noting that while the random perturbation technique converges more slowly, it yields lower losses and higher R values. In the realm of quantum information processing, trapped-ion systems have emerged as a premier platform for quantum computation and quantum simulation. To tackle larger-scale computational challenges, enhancing the coherence time of trapped ions is crucial. While recent experiments have improved the optical thickness of quantum plasma to near-unity to facilitate efficient light-ion interaction, creating a quantum plasma with inherently long coherence times remains difficult due to gas-source limitations in achieving both high optical thickness and low ion density simultaneously. This study introduces a novel method for generating quantum plasma using a quantum-turbulent Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). By initiating an explosion within the BEC using quantum fluctuations, this approach simultaneously maximizes optical thickness and minimizes incoherent interactions, thereby achieving an optimal trapped-ion quantum plasma with significantly prolonged coherence times. Numerical simulations demonstrate that ions generated via quantum turbulence achieve both high optical thickness and long coherence times, exhibiting optical thickness values up to 100 times greater than those produced by other gas-expansion methods. This work not only paves the way for large-scale quantum computation and simulation using quantum plasma but also offers fresh insights into the fundamental connection between Bose-Einstein condensation, quantum turbulence, and plasma formation.

This study demonstrates the creation of a quantum plasma with optimally prolonged coherence times by triggering a quantum-turbulent Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) with an explosion. This process simultaneously achieves high optical thickness and low incoherent interaction between atoms and ions, overcoming the traditional limitations of gas-source methods in balancing these factors. The approach leverages the unique properties of quantum fluctuations to initiate explosive expansion, thereby maximizing both optical thickness and coherence times from the outset. Numerical simulations reveal that this method can achieve optical thickness values up to 100 times higher than those limited by gas-expansion methods, confirming its efficacy in producing a quantum plasma with significantly enhanced coherence capabilities.

While many studies have explored learning in various conditions, a unified framework for efficiently learning tasks across diverse contexts and difficulty levels remains absent. This paper introduces the concept of Cross Learning (CrL), a general framework designed to acquire tasks from demonstrations of multiple contexts and difficulty levels. CrL utilizes three distinct types of contextual information: feasibility, desirability, and history. To manage different difficulty levels, the framework employs three learning processes based on structural similarity (SS), feature similarity (FS), and task similarity (TS). These processes are trained in sequence, with each building upon the previous to progressively refine the robustness of CrL. The proposed CrL approach was evaluated across numerous tasks in a diverse range of contexts, including human, expert-roboticist, and novice-roboticist demonstrations. Results demonstrated that CrL achieved high success rates for all methods, attaining near-100% success when incorporating FE and HF contextual data. Furthermore, the study highlighted that CrL enhances the generalization capability of individual learning methods. Robotic task learning via demonstration remains one of the primary methodologies in robotics for acquiring new skills. Although numerous techniques exist for incorporating Feasibility (FE), Desirability (DE), and History (HF) contextual constraints into single learning frameworks, very few address the acquisition of tasks from multiple difficulty levels. Given that DE is subjective to the demonstrator, demonstrations of the same task can vary significantly in difficulty. Furthermore, Feasibility, DE, and HF are interdependent; consequently, LfD techniques relying solely on FE often fail to generate optimal policies when high-quality demonstrations (compliant with FE, DE, and HF) are unavailable. To overcome these limitations, this work proposes CrL, a framework that leverages contextual constraints from multiple difficulty levels to robustly learn tasks across diverse scenarios. To do so, CrL trains three methods sequentially: first using only FE, then FE combined with DE, and finally FE, DE, and HF. The approach also innovates by incorporating CrL to enhance the generalization of traditional LfD techniques that depend exclusively on FE. However, training deep encoder models alongside the recurrent decoder states is computationally demanding. This paper introduces the concept of self-MLPs for embedded feature extraction. To facilitate this, we design an efficient self-MLP layer that utilizes self-attention to compute internal layer representations for extracting fixed features. Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) are frequently employed as fixed feature extractors in attention-based neural state-space models for sequence labeling. Nevertheless, jointly training deep encoder networks with recurrent decoders presents significant computational challenges. To address this, we propose the self-MLP for efficient embedded feature extraction. Specifically, we develop a static batch size masking strategy and input-dependent attention mechanism to accelerate the training of MLP layers. We validate our approach using the CoNLL-2003 Named Entity Recognition task, demonstrating that our method yields a model with competitive performance and substantially faster gradient and inference training speeds. Our results confirm the efficacy of self-MLPs for independent feature extraction and highlight the broader applicability of this technique. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ashwinr12/Self-MLP. Additionally, we provide git implementations of standard MLP and attention layers to assist with replication and experimentation.

By utilizing joint generalized coordinates as features, the method achieves parameterized action recognition, where the motion state is explicitly represented within the generalized coordinate space. (VPPMs) are emerging techniques that alter human perception to achieve specific objectives, such as misleading individuals about physical realities or influencing behavior. However, the underlying mechanisms of these phenomena remain poorly understood. This study investigates the informational dynamics within VPPMs to derive general insights into their function. We begin by defining an informational framework for perceiving and physically interacting with environments, specifically examining bending light-based stimuli (light funnels) and temperature-based manipulations (thermal hats). By modeling environmental information flow using channel capacity, we quantify the subjective and objective impacts of these techniques. Consistent with intuitive expectations, increasing channel capacity amplifies the influence of physical manipulations; conversely, significant disparities in channel capacity between manipulated and non-manipulated conditions result in strong perceptual illusions. Furthermore, analyzing environment information content reveals that perceptual distortions in manipulated zones are most pronounced when object information content is low. Finally, evaluating subjective and objective information alignment demonstrates that subjective perceptions can diverge from objective data, particularly under strong perceptual manipulation influence. Overall, we present a quantitative analysis of various VPPM effects grounded in information theory, revealing that these techniques operate by fundamentally restructuring environmental information flows to achieve their intended outcomes. Furthermore, this research establishes a methodology for analyzing a broad spectrum of environmental physical manipulations through an informational framework.

This study examines the elements influencing the model's language adaptability and analyzes the trade-offs between computational expenses and anticipated performance. Our findings indicate that the language adaptation process typically necessitates four times more data than the base language. Furthermore, we observe that simply transferring the vocabulary is inadequate; the statistical distribution of tokens must also be aligned. Additionally, we propose that the primary barrier to language adaptation is the model's inherent inductive bias toward its original language. To address this, we introduce a novel technique called Original-Lang Disruption (OLD), which impairs the model's proficiency in its initial language during pretraining to enhance sensitivity to new languages. Our results demonstrate that OLD effectively diminishes the model's bias toward its original language without significantly compromising performance in existing languages. Consequently, OLD enables the model to achieve comparable performance in newly added languages, even those with data distributions distinct from the training set. Collectively, our contributions outline the critical considerations for expanding a multilingual model's language coverage regarding both infrastructure and code. We anticipate that our insights will benefit the language adaptation processes of various large-scale models and systems. We examine two specific systems: the Proof System Logic (PSL), a normal, complete, and canonical propositional logic designed to characterize SAT, and the FinST, a finitely based, uniform, and complete algebraic normal form for boolean functions. While PSL has long been recognized as the logical counterpart to SAT, the existence of an algebraic analogue has remained an open question. In this work, we introduce a normal, complete, and uniform logical normal form for SAT that is inherently tied to a specific finite model theory logic. Furthermore, we analyze the polynomial time reducibility between SAT and SAT, and between FinST and FinST, through the lens of appropriate proof systems. Our approach leverages the concept of logical interpretability, which facilitates a direct investigation of interpretability within finite models. We also establish that every uniform proof system for SAT can be converted into an equivalent finitely based, consistent, and complete proof system. Additionally, we explore the interpretability relationships among various uniform proof systems for SAT. Finally, we investigate the interactions between finite model theory logics and consistent, complete, and finitely based proof systems for SAT, revealing that the finite model theory component corresponds to query evaluation via combined, uniform, and positive reductions, while the consistent, complete, and finitely based aspects of other proof systems for SAT remain largely unresolved. Consequently, we extend the inquiry into the relationships between established complexity classes of finite model theory. Specifically, we investigate the polynomial time reducibility between consistent, complete, and finitely based proof systems for SAT. Although we cannot yet determine if every consistent, complete, and finitely based proof system for SAT is either reducible to or capable of reducing every other such system, we establish that every consistent, complete, and finitely based proof system for SAT reduces to another in this category. By formalizing adversarial training as training on a distribution $\mathcal{D}'$ derived from the natural distribution $\mathcal{D}$ through $\epsilon$-ball perturbations, we demonstrate that the adversarial view constitutes a straightforward special case of domain adaptation. Specifically, we analyze three scenarios: (1) known but unobservable adversarial inputs (infeasible without labels); (2) known and observable inputs (practically viable); and (3) unknown inputs (practically feasible). For cases (1) and (2), we show that standard domain adaptation algorithms can effectively transfer existing results. In case (3), we demonstrate that Bayesian perspective offers new insights into designing more robust models. In this context, we propose approximating the posterior distribution $p(\mathbf{w}|S_\mathcal{D}', \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{U}'} )$ using variational inference. We validate these results experimentally by evaluating adversial training on the MNIST dataset. The findings indicate that Bayesian-based adversial training yields models with superior robustness compared to previous approaches, without compromising generalization performance. Furthermore, we explore methods for automatic learning of the radius parameter $\epsilon$. Our results suggest that learning these radii is not only feasible but can enhance robustness. Finally, we examine the relationship between Bayesian adversarial training and recent advances in adversarial regularization. Although Bayesian training with and without adversarial examples are distinct tasks, they share significant similarities. We propose a novel Bayesian adversarial regularization framework, noting that these methodologies are mutually informative. For instance, relaxing constraints in Bayesian adversial training aligns with removing constraints in adversarial regularization. Consequently, we establish a clear connection between these two perspectives, unlocking new results in adversarial regularization. Although learning the radius parameter $\epsilon$ is challenging, our experiments show that learning multiple radii is feasible. This approach enables the training of models robust to a broad spectrum of attacks. We conclude with future directions within the Bayesian framework. Our source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/aryaman97/Adversarial-Training-from-Bayesian-Perspective}. The paper will be submitted to JMLR. The title will be finalized at that time.

We introduce a many-body approach to decoupling interactions that, when applied to the effective model of itinerant electrons derived from the original repulsive Coulomb Hamiltonian, guarantees positivity of the resulting interaction terms. Utilizing the nonperturbative mapping of the original Hamiltonian to this effective form, we evaluate the decoupled interaction strength nonperturbatively. These steps enable a systematic analysis of how the dimensionality of the Coulomb interaction affects electronic phases and gaps. Our results indicate that while the two-dimensional effective Hubbard model featuring a dimensional-reduced Coulomb interaction preserves a Mott gap, the resulting electronic system exhibits complexity comparable to the original Hamiltonian's, including phase separation at short ranges and a metallic phase at large distances. In contrast, the model dimensional-reduced Coulomb interaction fails to sustain the Mott gap in the one-dimensional case, resulting in a gapped metallic phase at large interaction strengths. These findings highlight that the competition between the kinetic energy dimensionality and the Coulomb interaction dimensionality governs the phase diagram of one-dimensional itinerant electron systems with Coulomb interactions. Furthermore, we show that the magnitude of the Mott gap in the original two-dimensional model can be systematically controlled by the dimensional-reduced Coulomb interaction in the dimensional-reduced effective Hubbard model. These insights are applicable to various strongly correlated electron systems, such as doped antiferromagnetic insulators and high-temperature superconductors. Finally, the positive nature of the decoupled interaction terms provides a foundation for calculating the effective Hamiltonian's properties nonperturbatively. This finding addresses an outstanding theoretical challenge in the exact solution of strongly correlated electron systems and advances the theoretical understanding of strong correlations.

Existing approaches typically select the most uncertain instances from unlabeled data as queries; however, manual labeling of large volumes of uncertain data is costly and time-consuming. To address this, we introduce conditional active learning (CondAL), which posits that samples with low relevance to the target task should be excluded even if they exhibit high uncertainty. For each process, a partition $\Pi_n$ at time $n$ evolves from $\Pi_{n-1}$ by selecting a random element $i_n \in \mathbb{N}$ and either attaching it to a randomly chosen existing block or creating a new block $\{i_n\}$. The selection of $i_n$ follows a reinforcement mechanism with $\alpha > 0$, meaning $\mu(i) \propto i^{\alpha}$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. Once $i_n$ is determined, its integration into the partition occurs via attachment to a previous block with probability proportional to $2^{-j}$ if $i_n > j$, or it forms a new block of $\{i_n\}$ with the remaining probability.

We demonstrate that these processes satisfy a scaling limit theorem analogous to that found in the Chinese Restaurant Process. Specifically, we prove that the proportion of partitions containing exactly $k$ elements is asymptotically distributed according to a Borel distribution with index $\alpha+1$. Furthermore, these dynamics exhibit characteristics typically associated with preferential attachment models. By adapting methods from the literature, we establish that the probability a vertex of degree $k$ remains unpaired is asymptotically proportional to $k^{2-\alpha}$ for $\alpha < 3$, and that degree distributions follow a power law for $\alpha > 1$. Additionally, we utilize differential equations to derive asymptotic expectations and strengthen these results using large deviation principles. Finally, we numerically simulate three specific processes—where $\mu(i) = i^2$, $\mu(i) = i$, and $\mu(i) = 1$—to empirically validate the theoretical predictions and observe the typical graph structure resulting from these processes. To our knowledge, this represents the first research demonstrating the convergence of a random partition process, which combines both cutting and merging mechanisms, to a random tree.

Shape completion involves recovering a full 3D object from partial scans by optimizing parameters that maximize a reward function designed to ensure closure under symmetry or continuity. However, because reward functions rely on local gradients, agents struggle to grasp global closure principles unless explicitly programmed, necessitating extensive exploration of the parameter space. Generalization to novel tasks is accomplished via few-shot learning by gathering new annotated data using the same features as the original task. Furthermore, we establish that such adversarial policies exhibit zero robustness, aligning with a newly proven complexity lower bound. To address this, we introduce a robust on-policy learning algorithm capable of withstanding adversarial interference. Empirical results indicate that our method maintains resilience against adversarial attacks and surpasses existing offline approaches in various reward scenarios. In supervised learning, adversarial examples are well-documented, yet their existence and impact in off-policy reinforcement learning remain less clear. This raises critical questions for offline RL: Can an adversary who cannot alter the state-reward distribution still drive learned policies to perform at random? Can they force learned policies to adopt specific target behaviors? And can they improve a policy relative to a target? We answer these in the affirmative. Specifically, we adapt a prior adversarial example construction to derive a generalization result for offline RL, establishing that the robustness complexity of offline RL matches that of supervised learning. Our approach involves two key steps: first, we construct adversarial examples under minimal assumptions about the RL environment's structure, and second, we argue that these examples generalize to arbitrary environments. This result has two implications. First, it reveals that offline RL is equally vulnerable to adversarial examples as standard supervised learning. Second, it suggests that designing adversarial defenses for offline RL should benefit from techniques already developed for environments subject to minimal adversarial attacks. Consequently, this research should motivate the creation of more robust offline RL algorithms.

Adversarial examples and attacks are well-documented in supervised learning, where inputs are intentionally perturbed to mislead neural network classifiers. In reinforcement learning (RL), analogous adversarial examples involve perturbations of environments, while those of value functions aim to inflate state values to prevent convergence. In this paper, we investigate adversarial attacks within offline RL. We propose three environments where the optimal policy for the unadversarial environment is provably distinct from that of the adversarial version. We propose the First Order of Derivative of Log-Probability (FODL) as a novel, straightforward, and effective method for OOD detection. The core concept of FODL is to measure the instability of the log-probability forecast generated by deep networks by analyzing the first-order derivative of this probability relative to model parameters. This approach leverages deep networks as density estimators and utilizes the sensitivity of their logarithmic probabilities to parametric variations as a proxy for estimation stability. Furthermore, we introduce an enhanced logarithmic transformation of model parameters to better highlight the most influential parameters. Extensive experiments across three visual tasks and two scenarios—OOD detection and outlier detection—demonstrate that FODL surpasses state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the method's effectiveness and illuminate its underlying mechanisms. The implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/ziqianliu2000/FODL. This paper presents an additional decidability result concerning transducers that approximate one-way transducers within the origin semantics framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is decidable whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an origin-equivalent one-way transducer via resynchronization by a bounded, regular resynchronizer. This finding contrasts sharply with standard semantics, where determining if a non-deterministic two-way transducer is equivalent to any one-way transducer remains undecidable. This study utilizes a combined dataset from the Keck/HIRES and HARP spectrographs to measure the system's total light and separate the individual spectra of the primary star and its companion. By employing radiative transfer modeling, we derive fundamental properties and an atmospheric structure for GJ 229B that aligns with existing literature, thereby validating our data reduction approach and instrumentation. Furthermore, we conduct a re-analysis of historical Spitzer Space Telescope data to determine the companion's heat redistribution pattern. Based on our findings, we propose a highly efficient redistribution mechanism for GJ 229B, consistent with the generally poor redistribution observed in brown dwarfs. We finalize our results by comparing the re-analyzed Spitzer photometry with recent data from the James Webb Space Telescope.

While no single mathematical model adequately captures all physical phenomena and boundary conditions, the OpenFOAM toolkit provides a comprehensive framework for simulating these dynamics. \begin{abstract}
This paper presents a construction of "nonlocal" constants of motion for Euler-Lagrange ODEs. As an application, we review the existence of global solutions for dissipative oscillators and derive estimates for these solutions by adapting the "nonlocal" constants of motion from \cite{DLMR}. Additionally, we apply this theory to the Euler-Poisson equations of a heavy top and the Euler-Lagrange equations of a relativistic particle. Furthermore, we determine the existence of "nonlocal" constants of motion for specific PDEs, including the Euler equations of ideal hydrodynamics and the Yo-Yo equations. Finally, we situate this research within the broader context of literature on "nonlocal" constants of motion.

Keywords: Euler-Lagrange ODEs, first integrals, nonlocal constants of motion, Euler-Lagrange PDEs, jet spaces, Legendre transform.

We introduce a algorithm for reconstructing plane graphs from (noisy) measurements of their associated electrical currents. Specifically, given $K$ distinct electrical flows on a weighted planar graph $G$, we prove that sampling the current passing through $O(K (\log \mathrm{card}(V)))$ randomly selected edges suffices to reconstruct $G$ in expected polynomial time. However, computing DTW distances between two sequences typically requires $O(nm)$ time, where $n$ and $m$ represent the lengths of the respective sequences. While existing exact indexings or algorithms for DTW-based similarity search or clustering offer theoretical improvements to this complexity, no current method achieves linear time complexity relative to a single sequence length. We introduce the Breakpoint Index (BPIndex), a novel indexing structure designed for efficient DTW similarity search. When $k=1$, this reduces to $O(n)$. We validate BPIndex's efficiency on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it can search a collection of one million sequences in under ten minutes. Additionally, we employ statistical analysis of the breakpoint index to explain its asymptotic average-case complexity. Comparisons with other indexing structures or algorithms reveal that BPIndex outperforms them by more than an order of magnitude. CPs can achieve more than their share of the profits by incentivizing ISPs to raise investment levels, while ISPs can negotiate multiple agreements simultaneously to maximize profit improvements above the non-cooperative baseline. We analyze how the complexity of user utility functions—specifically the number of parameters—affects the feasibility and optimality of these profit-sharing contracts. Our results indicate that simpler parameter forms favor CPs, whereas more complex parameter forms benefit ISPs. Furthermore, we propose mechanisms for ISPs to optimize their investment decisions by negotiating simultaneous agreements with the CP, demonstrating that these mechanisms enable ISPs to increase their own investments, raise user quality of experience (QoE), and secure above-equilibrium profits. Finally, we present a parameterized game-theoretic model of network investment that we solve for the Nash equilibrium.

We develop a compartmental disease transmission model tailored to a small population in Central America suffering from a high burden of infectious diseases. This model investigates scenarios involving total lockdowns as a response to outbreaks and includes formulations that account for fluctuating population sizes and resource constraints, resulting in population and resource-balanced models designed for humanitarian applications. Following model derivation, we introduce a parameterization strategy grounded in outbreak data and an algorithm specifically suited for multi-resource, time-dependent parameter estimation. The paper concludes with examples and simulations that assess these model formulations and solution methods under conditions of high population mobility and resource variation, which are common in many humanitarian contexts. Abstract Attention maps offer a transparent mechanism for understanding deep neural networks by linking input features to outputs. However, current attention maps remain limited because existing loss functions fail to enforce desirable attributes aligned with human preferences. To address this, we develop novel loss functions incorporating three such attributes: spatial consistency, coarse-to-fine ordering, and object completeness. The first loss encourages attention to remain focused on objects across different scales, while the second ensures attention expands from coarse to fine co-ordinates as prediction confidence grows. The third loss maintains object completeness within the predicted segmentation by leveraging class-specific anchors in 3D space. Our experiments confirm that these loss functions effectively induce the desired attributes in attention maps and enhance semantic segmentation accuracy. At ICCV 2021, we achieved a mIoU of 68.1% on the Pascal VOC 2012 dataset using only 20 training images per class, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline. Additionally, using 100 images per class, we obtained an mIoU of 75.8% on the ADE20K dataset, once again exceeding the baseline results.

This paper focuses on two specific types of topological phenomena: (i) chiral anomaly-induced Hall effects in three-dimensional (3D) topological insulators under external electric and magnetic fields, and (ii) topological magnetic insulators—charge-neutral systems such as neutron stars or cold neutron gases in neutron-optical cavities—exhibiting planar Hall effects driven by the anomaly in spatially varying pseudofields. We anticipate that investigating the topological aspects of these systems will provide crucial insights into their fundamental properties. Furthermore, our findings may facilitate the development of novel methods for experimentally verifying topological phenomena in 3D topological insulators through the observation of Hall effects. Additionally, these results could aid in creating theoretical frameworks for understanding topological phenomena in various fields, including condensed matter physics, cosmology, and quantum field theory. Finally, we expect these findings to contribute to the advancement of a new field emerging at the intersection of condensed matter physics and topological insulators exhibiting planar Hall effects. Given the potential for experimental verification in neutron stars, we also consider these results as contributing factors to the field of astrophysical plasma physics.

Our investigation into the topological aspects of these systems led to the following contributions. Regarding chiral anomaly-induced Hall effects in 3D topological insulators, we derived the effect under external electric and magnetic fields using the semiclassical method based on the effective action of quasiparticles within the Dirac model. This derived result provides new insights into the topological nature of chiral anomaly effects in such systems. In terms of topological magnetic insulators, we examined the planar Hall effect generated by the pseudofield in space. We demonstrated that the coefficient of this planar Hall effect serves as an topological invariant linked to the pseudofield and can be calculated using a formulation analogous to that of the ordinary Hall effect. We anticipate that analyzing the chiral anomaly effect under external electric and magnetic fields, as well as the planar Hall effect in systems with nontrivial pseudofields, will offer valuable insights into the fundamental properties and potential experimental detection of topological phenomena in both neutron stars and laboratory settings. These contributions are directly applicable to the experimental verification of chiral anomaly effects in 3D topolar insulators and the investigation of planar Hall effects

Experimental results confirm that GTNs perform on par with GNNs in time series and image classification, yet they significantly outperform GNNs in molecular property prediction. der$ and $Wilson$ algorithms are prominent methods for generating uniform spanning trees (USTs) using random walks. This study examines their interplay to accelerate the construction of random trees. By analyzing $branches$—specific paths produced by both algorithms at defined stopping times—we demonstrate that the trees generated on a complete graph are distributionally equivalent at these moments. We present an algorithm named $Branch$, which utilizes $m$ branches to create $n$-node random trees in $O(m+n)$ time. When $m$ scales logarithmically with $n$ and the expected edge count is minimized, the resulting tree possesses $O(n\log(\log(n)))$ edges. Similarly, the $Branch$ algorithm and the $Aldous\text{-}Broder$ algorithm yield random bridges on graphs distributed identically. We evaluate the expected $6$th power of the bridge length for both algorithms, a metric critical for bounding the algorithm's performance. Although $Branch$ is more efficient at predicting the bridge's length, $Aldous\text{-}Broder$ excels in predicting the bridge's distribution. Finally, we investigate the distribution and expected lengths of random bridges on an $N$-node Galton-Watson tree with cutoff. While $Aldous\text{-}Broder$ remains more effective here, the $Branch$ algorithm performs competitively when $N$ is small. Furthermore, we observe that the expected bridge length produced by $Branch$ is shorter than that of $Wilson$ in most scenarios.

Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a widely used algorithm for aligning temporal sequences. While various optimizations have enhanced its efficiency, it remains a dynamic programming method that must explore a large portion of the distance matrix to identify optimal alignments. This paper introduces an approach that accelerates DTW by representing time series as sparse vectors. This method leverages existing sparsity techniques, such as Iterative Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS), to accelerate an algorithm proposed by Keogh et al. Additionally, we develop an adaptive strategy to determine the minimum number of iterations required for approximation. Experimental results indicate that, compared to standard DTW, our proposed methods achieve speedups of up to 100x while maintaining alignment quality within 5% of the optimal solution. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to evaluate the effects of sparsity, application domain, series length, and other factors on both alignment quality and computational speed. To support reproducibility, the R package "spDTW" is available at <https://github.com/davidebaldi/spDTW>.

We present an algorithm designed to identify near-duplicate web pages without relying on page titles or external data. Traditional methods, such as Shasha's technique, rely on edit distance to compare web pages in linear time relative to their size. However, these approaches typically compare every page against every other page within a collection, resulting in a computational cost proportional to the square of the total number of pages. Our method diverges from this paradigm by utilizing sentence-level data and the inverted file structure common in search engines. By mapping each word to its corresponding page, we enable rapid identification of pages sharing specific content. We evaluate the method's accuracy and precision using the DMT dataset and compare its performance shorthands with Shasha's technique. Our findings demonstrate that our approach achieves a 2000x speedup over Shasha's method while maintaining within 2% of the maximum possible alignment quality.

This paper introduces a multi-task learning approach designed to assist human domain experts in effectively calibrating task relevance and data selection during joint modeling of human preferences and machine performance. We formulate guidance as a collaborative effort between a human expert and a learning algorithm, where the expert manually estimates task relevance for specific data points without explicitly defining all tasks, while the learning algorithm identifies outliers in human feedback to ensure representative data coverage. The widespread adoption of social media has led to an explosion of information being shared online. While this content offers significant value, it also brings challenges related to privacy, security, and trust. This document examines these issues and potential solutions, drawing on examples from research and industry to highlight the complexities involved. We also discuss how these problems evolve over time as the nature of page content shifts. Ultimately, we propose several directions for future work. This paper is part of a series resulting from a workshop on Long-Lived Pages, organized by the Information Integration Institute (I4P) during the ISWC conferences in 2012 and 2013. These activities are expected to be crucial as pages age and as new standards emerge. Additionally, we explore issues of page management and control, considering how pages are created and who is responsible for them. The discussion on security and privacy addresses risks faced by page owners and their communities, as well as broader public privacy concerns. Regarding storage and retrieval, we examine challenges concerning page persistence and their integration into information systems. This paper presents an entirely general rigorous coupled-wave approach for homogeneous bianisotropic metagratings embedded in homogeneous fluids. By employing a rigorous unit-cell analysis, we derive complete boundary conditions and mode-matching equations for the unit cell, thereby forming the foundation of our method. Our theory operates within an entirely numerical framework without requiring any approximate unit-cell models. We primarily apply this framework to sound-hard metagratings, demonstrating its utility through various examples, including calculating the internal pressure field within a unit cell and accurately predicting far-field scattering for highly modulated structures where ray acoustics would fail. Furthermore, we utilize these general analytical tools to theoretically design and predict perfect absorption in Bianisotropic metagratings. Finally, we enhance existing theories for unidirectional metagratings by deriving enhanced boundary conditions and approximate periodic multi-scale models for homogeneous media containing Bianisotropic inclusions. Because these enhanced models are not restricted to weak modulations, they hold potential for significantly improving current methods for sound-hard and weakly modulated metagratings. The formulated theories can be readily adapted for analogous electromagnetic scenarios. Furthermore, the general boundary conditions derived herein hold broad interest as they may be directly utilized to construct entirely general numerical methods for homogeneous Bianisotropic metagratings using finite-element or finite-difference time-domain techniques. Consequently, an entirely general method for such structures may now be achievable via multiple distinct theoretical pathways. These findings establish the basis for entirely general rigorous designs of Bianisotropic acousto-optical metagratings for precise and flexible control of unit-cell internal fields and acoustic wave propagation in fluids. This enables the full exploitation of the unique physical properties of such metagratings to achieve applications previously beyond reach. Furthermore, the theories of general Bianisotropic acoustic metagratings may now facilitate the explanation and design of various recently demonstrated experimental results. This capability represents a crucial advancement in the emerging experimental science of general acoustic metagratings. In summary, general designs of acoustic metagratings were previously impossible due to a lack of theoretical tools; however, the theories presented herein now render this a reality. Specifically, it is difficult to achieve sample-efficient learning in complex, high-dimensional navigation tasks without assuming dynamic similarities between simulation and reality. We address this by introducing a new framework that leverages isotonic regression to create an implicit simulation for training physics-aware policies directly on real robots. During interaction, we simultaneously gather robot data and conduct standard model-free learning. Our approach achieves strong sample efficiency by rapidly converging to a near-optimal solution through a parallel simulation, thereby facilitating real-time deployment. Empirical evaluations using a high-degree-of-freedom human torso demonstrate the method's efficacy: it learns a skill to perform push-ups within 1000 physical trials, resulting in a 2-5 fold improvement over zero-transfer fine-tuning methods, and outperforms episodic simulation learning by up to 10 times to match real-world performance. This represents, to our knowledge, the most sample-efficient continuous control skill ever learned solely on a human torso. To promote reproducibility, we will open-source all algorithms and hardware involved. Overall, our work demonstrates that an agent can acquire a novel task from a "blank slate," rapidly generalize to real robots, transfer directly to a human, teach individuals how to perform push-ups, adapt to varying capabilities, recover from disruptions, and enable rapid multi-task learning. We believe this research has broad implications for diverse fields requiring physical deployment, including assistive and rehabilitative robotics. These findings complement the additive scenario addressed in arXiv:1808.00881, thereby completing the picture of linear combinations of multiplicative functions. Specifically, they confirm a long-standing conjecture regarding the accuracy with which Riemann's zeta function can model the $t$-central moments of multiplicative functions. This result validates Montgomery--Vaughan type estimates, enabling the derivation of precise value distribution descriptions for these functions.

Furthermore, these conclusions support Sarnak's conjecture, demonstrating that multiplicative functions exhibiting strong non-vanishing properties give rise to $L$-functions $L(s, \chi)$ with a slope that closely mirrors Riemann's zeta function. This finding underscores the pivotal role zeta functions play in governing the arithmetic properties of multiplicative sequences. Additionally, the analysis uncovers a broad family of functional equations with a slope nearly identical to that of Riemann's zeta function, providing further evidence linking the analytic and arithmetic domains. These results also constitute a significant advancement toward Titchmarsh's zero-density estimate. Finally, the discussion offers a natural extension of the concept of natural boundaries in complex analysis.

Currently, only a non-effective bound for k as a function of k+|2A+A|-3k exists. However, for a fixed integer k, there exist infinite families of "nearly" APs of cardinality k that are closed under addition and possess a set of additions with size 2k-1, where the union of these families is not an AP. Consequently, the paper proposes a new formulation of Freiman's theorem for addition bases of order 1, which replaces arbitrary subsets with additive bases. Specifically, additive bases of small size that are closed under addition are demonstrated to be nested sums of Nielsen's infinite family of nilpotent Lie rings of class 1, characterized by specific parameters. To establish the theorem, effective bounds for additive versions of Szemerédi's arithmetic progression theorem (proven by Davenport and Roth) and a recent expansion theorem for nilpotent Lie rings (established by the authors) are utilized. Ultimately, this approach yields an effective version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem within the context of additive bases, thereby addressing a concern raised by Blagojevic and others, and providing one of two known effective formulations of Freiman's theorem for analytic number theory. To support this, the author introduces an infinite family of Nielsen's Lie rings to construct infinite sets of counterexamples for cardinality k where the set of additions is merely closed under addition, rendering the strict statement of the theorem false. Furthermore, the author demonstrates that a sufficient condition for effectiveness is replacing "cardinality k" with "additive basis of size 2k-1," resulting in a novel effective version of Freiman's theorem for analytic number theory. This new formulation is argued to be stronger than the recent effective approaches by Croot and by Li and Shparlinski, both of which were designed to provide distinct applications. This formulation is referred to as the "Additive Basis Theorem." Finally, the paper provides novel applications of this theorem, including a novel application of the polynomial method to analytic number theory, which derives the effective Koukouvinou-Tsang configuration theorem from the additive basis of small size closed under addition, alongside an infinite family of counterexamples to a conjecture by Louwak and Shparlinski. While the weak equivalence principle predicts a linear relationship between gravitational redshift and local gravitational acceleration, a specific class of nonweak theories anticipates deviations characterized by a nonzero coefficient for a $g^{-1}$ term. Although previous research generally concludes that the weak equivalence principle is robust, the LECGRS dataset, comprising 14 microwave laser ranging experiments conducted on the Moon where redshift is inferred from total range residuals after modeling all other effects, offers a complementary test capable of identifying nonlinearity. Our results indicate a residual gravitational redshift signal of $1.5\% \pm 0.9\%$ of the weak equivalence principle prediction with a significance level of $2.2\sigma$. However, this detection could be attributed to unmodeled range errors, rendering the result inconsistent with predictions derived from weak equivalence theories or other prior tests. Consequently, this measurement serves as an upper limit on the linearity of the weak equivalence principle that is approximately an order of magnitude more restrictive than all prior range-based measurements. Finally, we outline future plans to utilize long-baseline integrals of the LECGRS data for testing postweak equivalence theories featuring nonuniversal composition dependence. Integrating this approach with planetary ephemerides analyses will further constrain planscalar curvature coupling and dipolar modification parameters associated with postweak theories. Since integrating the range into a joint analysis is computationally and conceptually more complex than analyzing the range integral separately, this strategy represents a pathway to achieve orders-of-magnitude improvements over current limits.

Unlike other recommendation approaches, this paradigm is more susceptible to data sparsity because it relies on very limited short-term user activity. To address this limitation, we introduce a new session-based recommendation framework called \textit{Meta-Session}. The core of this model is a meta-model that generates session-specific embeddings through dynamic weighting of component models. Unlike previous methods relying on fixed weights, our meta-model leverages session uniqueness to enhance performance. Specifically, we employ session variety to construct diverse features, aiming to improve the model's capacity to capture varied session characteristics. Furthermore, we utilize session similarity to build an ensemble of classifiers, thereby boosting robustness against label noise. Extensive experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that Meta-Session significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art DeepWalk model. Furthermore, we provide detailed ablation studies and visualizations of the meta-model's weights to offer valuable insights into optimizing session-based recommendations. To our knowledge, this is the first work to employ meta-learning within the domain of session-based recommendation. To sum up, our primary contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item We propose Meta-Session, the inaugural application of meta-learning to session-based recommendation.
    \item We introduce novel techniques to strengthen session variety and similarity, enhancing both the meta-model's capability to capture diversity and its robustness to label noise.
    \item Our model delivers a substantial improvement in AUC compared to prior state-of-the-art methods.
    \item We provide detailed ablation studies and visualizations of the meta-model's weights to offer insights into session-based recommendation.
